lede: Most questions about data start with "only the rows where…". In PySpark that's `filter`: you describe a condition, and Spark keeps the rows where it's true.
objectives: Keep the rows that match a condition with `filter` (or its twin, `where`)
Write conditions with `F.col`, comparisons and `isin`, on text, numbers and dates
Combine conditions with `&`, `|` and `~`, wrapping each one in parentheses
Predict which rows a filter keeps, including rows with a missing value

blocks.md:
The `orders` table above has one row per order in a small shop. In every example on this page it's already loaded as a DataFrame called `orders`, and `F` is `pyspark.sql.functions`, the usual short name.

`orders.filter(condition)` gives back a **new** DataFrame with only the rows where `condition` is true. The columns stay exactly as they were, and `orders` itself doesn't change. A condition is built from a column, written `F.col("name")`, and a comparison.

blocks.title: Keep only the paid orders
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

paid = orders.filter(F.col("status") == "paid")
paid.show()
blocks.note: Four of the twelve orders are paid. `show()` prints the rows, so you can see what the filter kept: all six columns, untouched.

blocks.md:
The comparisons are the ones you know from Python: `==`, `!=`, `>`, `>=`, `<` and `<=`. They work on text, on numbers like `total`, and on dates. For a date column, write the date as text in `"YYYY-MM-DD"` form and Spark compares it as a date.

Text comparisons are exact: `"Paid"` is not `"paid"`.

blocks.title: Compare numbers and dates
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

big = orders.filter(F.col("total") >= 200)
big.select("order_id", "status", "total").show()

early = orders.filter(F.col("order_date") < "2026-02-01")
early.select("order_id", "order_date").show()
blocks.note: `select` (lesson 9) only trims what's printed here; the filter decides which rows there are. `>=` keeps a total of exactly 200; `>` wouldn't.

blocks.md: To ask for two things at once, combine conditions with `&` (and) or `|` (or). **Put each condition in its own parentheses.** Python works out `&` and `|` before `==` and `>=`, so without parentheses it combines the wrong pieces.

blocks.title: Two conditions at once
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

paid_in_app = orders.filter((F.col("status") == "paid") & (F.col("channel") == "app"))
paid_in_app.select("order_id", "status", "channel").show()

store_or_big = orders.filter((F.col("channel") == "store") | (F.col("total") >= 250))
store_or_big.select("order_id", "channel", "total").show()
blocks.note: With `&` a row must pass both conditions; with `|` either one is enough.

blocks.title: Forgetting the parentheses
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

orders.filter(F.col("status") == "paid" & F.col("total") >= 100).show()
blocks.note: Without parentheses Python reads this as one long chain and asks a column for a plain `True` or `False`, which it can't give. The same error appears if you write Python's `and` or `or` between conditions: on columns, always use `&` and `|`.

blocks.md: When the allowed values are a list, `isin` is shorter than several `==` joined with `|`. Put `~` in front of a condition to turn it around: `~` means "not".

blocks.title: A list of values, and not
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

on_the_way = orders.filter(F.col("status").isin("paid", "shipped"))
on_the_way.select("order_id", "status").show()

kept = orders.filter(~F.col("status").isin("cancelled", "refunded"))
print(kept.count(), "of", orders.count(), "orders were not cancelled or refunded")
blocks.note: `count()` counts the rows of a DataFrame.

blocks.md:
`where` is the same method as `filter` under another name, so `orders.where(F.col("status") == "paid")` gives the same rows.

One more rule matters with real data: **a comparison with a missing value isn't true.** If an order's `total` is missing, `F.col("total") >= 100` is not true for it, so `filter` drops that row. Lesson 19 shows how to find and handle missing values on purpose.

concept.prompt: Which line keeps the paid orders with a total of at least 100?
concept.why: Each condition needs its own parentheses, joined with `&`. Without parentheses, or with Python's `and`, PySpark raises an error; `|` would keep orders that pass either condition.

choices: A new DataFrame with the web orders and all of orders' columns
Nothing: it removes the other rows from orders
A column of True and False values
Only the channel column, for web orders
concept.why: `filter` returns a new DataFrame with the matching rows and every column unchanged. `orders` itself stays as it was.

concept.prompt: An order's `total` is missing. Does `orders.filter(F.col("total") >= 100)` keep it?
choices: No: a comparison with a missing value isn't true, so the row is dropped
Yes, with the total changed to 0
concept.why: A comparison with a missing value is not true, so `filter` leaves the row out. No error is raised.

review: `df.filter(condition)` returns a new DataFrame with the rows where the condition is true. The columns don't change, and neither does `df`.
Build conditions from `F.col("name")` and `==`, `!=`, `>`, `>=`, `<`, `<=`. Compare a date column with a date written as `"YYYY-MM-DD"`.
`isin(...)` checks against a list of values, and `~` means not.
Join conditions with `&` (and) and `|` (or), each in its own parentheses. Python's `and` and `or` don't work on columns.
A comparison with a missing value isn't true, so `filter` drops that row.
